title: Macrina
hook: the older sister who taught her brothers Basil and Gregory, and led a community at home

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory of Nazianzus, and your line was peace over position. Did you step back from the fight you named? Day seven hundred seventy-five.

A heads-up about names. Yesterday's Gregory was Basil's friend from Nazianzus. Today there's another Gregory: Basil's younger brother, Gregory of Nyssa, also a bishop, also a deep writer. And both of those brothers had an older sister. Her name was Macrina. She never became a bishop. She didn't preach at councils. And yet her brother Gregory wrote her life, and wrote a whole book of conversation with her, and in it he hardly ever calls her by her name. He calls her the Teacher.

Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina tells it from the start. She was the eldest child. As a girl, she was engaged to a young man who died before the wedding. Her family wanted to arrange another match. She refused. In her view, Gregory says, she was still promised to him, a man alive to God, and she would wait for the resurrection. So she stayed home with her mother and the younger children. Then Basil came home from his studies. And here Gregory is startlingly frank about his famous brother. In paraphrase: Basil came back excessively proud of his skill as a speaker, looking down on everyone important in town. Macrina took him in hand. She drew him, Gregory says, toward a simpler life, away from fame, toward God. The Basil we met two days ago, kissing the sick outside his new city, had a sister behind him. Then Macrina turned her household into a community. She persuaded her mother to live on equal terms with the women who had been their servants: the same table, the same work, the same prayers. Rank dissolved around the dinner table. She also raised and taught her youngest brother, Peter, who became a bishop too. At the end of her life, Gregory came to see her, heavy with grief after Basil's death. She was dying, and she comforted him, and the two of them talked about the soul and the resurrection. He wrote it down as a dialogue, with her as the Teacher, and himself as the student who keeps asking questions. The teacher of teachers: a woman at home, teaching brothers who would go on to teach the church.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who was a Macrina for you. An older sister, maybe, or a cousin, an aunt, a neighbor, a coach, a coworker who showed you the ropes. Someone who taught you without a title, maybe even took you down a peg when you needed it. Let one person come. Remember one specific thing they did or said. Hold it. If you pray, you can thank God for them, by name. Then think of how you might thank them directly: a message, a call, a note. The bell holds the time.
Macrina. The older sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who drew her brothers toward God and led a community at home, and whom Gregory called the Teacher.
Your line: the teacher of teachers. Today, send the person you named a thank-you that mentions the one specific thing. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor Macrina as a saint, and Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina and his dialogue with her are read as spiritual classics.
